scenes.vo: This tortoise is believed to have hatched in eighteen thirty two. He is still alive.
scenes.cap: Believed to have hatched in 1832. Still alive.

scenes.vo: His name is Jonathan. He lives on the island of St Helena, and he's estimated to be one hundred and ninety four years old.
scenes.cap: Jonathan, St Helena: an estimated 194 years old

scenes.vo: Scientists studied his epigenome. Think of it as the switches that decide which genes are on and off.
scenes.cap: They studied his epigenome: the on/off switches for genes

scenes.vo: They found two hundred and eighty seven distinctive genetic variants.
And the gene regulators for energy production and DNA repair? Incredibly stable, after nearly two centuries.
scenes.cap: Regulators for energy + DNA repair: "incredibly stable"

scenes.vo: Repairing DNA damage is one of the main ways a body fights ageing. Jonathan seems to have kept that system running.
scenes.cap: DNA repair is a key defence against ageing

scenes.vo: It's the first epigenome study of a giant tortoise, in Science Advances. Hatched in eighteen thirty two. What's next?
